headline: Oil on edge, an asteroid crash site, and who really wrote that homework
teaser: Can words move oil prices? Is asteroid defence worth the money? And what is homework actually for?

articles.title: Pricing Fear: Why Oil Markets Swing on Diplomatic Headlines
articles.dek: Oil fell more than 7 percent in a day, yet not a single barrel had moved. Are markets smart, or just jumpy?
paras: On Monday, 2 November 2026, the world's two main oil prices suffered their steepest one-day fall in three months. West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the leading American benchmark, dropped 7.4 percent to settle at $96.46 a barrel, slipping below the symbolic $100 mark, while Brent crude, the international reference price, lost 7.6 percent to close at $104.77. Yet no new oil field had been found, and no tanker had changed course. What moved the market was a set of words: reports that Iran's supreme leader had approved negotiations with the United States, and that the American president wanted to give those talks a chance to play out.

To understand why words can be worth billions of dollars, it helps to recall how oil is priced. In the textbook model, the price of a commodity reflects the balance between supply and demand. Oil, however, is traded largely through futures contracts, which are agreements to buy or sell a fixed quantity at a set price on a future date. Because these contracts concern barrels that will be delivered weeks or months later, their price depends not only on today's physical market but also on traders' expectations about tomorrow. When there is a credible threat that supply could suddenly be cut off, buyers are willing to pay extra as a kind of insurance. Analysts call this additional cost the risk premium.

Since the conflict involving Iran began in late February, that premium has been unusually large. Roughly one-fifth of the oil the world consumes each day normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula, so any disruption there threatens supplies far beyond the region. Brent has swung between $72 and $126 a barrel during the conflict, and in October prices climbed to a six-month high as Gulf supplies came under pressure and Ukrainian drones struck Russian refineries. When diplomacy suddenly appeared possible, as one shipping analyst put it, "a lot of risk premium" began "seeping out" of the market.

The size of the fall, however, also had a mechanical cause. Many investment funds follow automated, trend-following strategies that buy when prices rise and sell when they fall. As the price of Brent began to drop, these traders reduced their bets on further increases, and their selling pushed prices lower still. In other words, the initial reaction to the news was amplified by the structure of the market itself.

For some observers, this episode shows that markets work efficiently. In their view, an oil price is simply a constantly updated estimate of risk: when war threatens supply, prices rise and encourage consumers to conserve and producers elsewhere to pump more; when the danger fades, prices fall again. The sharp drop, they argue, was a rational response to new information. Critics see something less reassuring. They point out that the underlying situation had barely changed, since the two sides had not even agreed on terms for fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and that the market seemed to be reacting "with extreme sensitivity to every headline," in the words of one bank analyst. If a single statement can erase more than seven percent of an asset's value in a day, they ask, how much do prices really reveal about physical supply?

The stakes are not merely academic. For ordinary households, oil prices feed directly into the cost of transport, heating and food. In the United States, the average price of regular gasoline stood at $4.17 a gallon at the start of November, compared with $3.04 a year earlier, and diesel, which is vital for trucks and farm machinery, averaged $6.29, up from $3.68. A lasting fall would offer real relief. Yet forecasters warned that the reprieve could be temporary. Goldman Sachs had recently raised its December forecast for Brent to $105 a barrel and cautioned that prices could average $130 next year if Gulf production remained far below its 2025 level.

High prices also involve a longer-term trade-off. Expensive fuel strengthens the economic case for electric vehicles and renewable energy, and some economists argue that price shocks speed up the energy transition. However, the burden of such shocks falls most heavily on low-income families and on developing countries that import most of their energy, which makes it difficult to treat volatility as a welcome policy tool.

On balance, the most persuasive reading is that both camps are partly right. The November fall did reflect a genuine reduction in perceived risk, but its scale owed much to the way modern markets magnify sentiment. Until the strait is fully reopened, oil prices are likely to keep reacting to headlines, and the decisive factor will not be what leaders say but whether tankers can move freely.

articles.title: A Crash-Site Investigation 197 Million Kilometres from Earth
articles.dek: Four years after NASA crashed into an asteroid, Hera has arrived to inspect the damage. Is planetary defence worth it?
paras: On the evening of 18 October 2026, a camera aboard the European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft captured an image that, to an untrained eye, looked unremarkable: a bright dot with a faint companion barely one pixel wide. For the mission team, however, the picture marked a milestone. Taken from 1,280 kilometres away, it was the first time Hera had resolved the binary asteroid system it was built to study into two separate objects: the 780-metre Didymos and its small moon, Dimorphos, which measures about 151 metres across, roughly the size of the Great Pyramid of Giza. "For the very first time we are seeing through Hera's own eyes the very double asteroid system that the mission was designed and built for," said mission manager Ian Carnelli.

Dimorphos is no ordinary moon. On 26 September 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) deliberately crashed into it at 6.1 kilometres per second. The collision hurled a plume of debris across some 10,000 kilometres of space and shortened Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes. It was the first time human effort had measurably shifted the orbit of a natural object in the Solar System. Neither asteroid posed any danger to Earth; the pair was chosen precisely because it offered a safe laboratory in which a small orbital change could be measured with telescopes on the ground.

The experiment tested a strategy known as kinetic impact. If an asteroid were found to be on a collision course with Earth, a spacecraft could strike it years in advance, nudging it just enough that a tiny change in velocity would grow into a miss of thousands of kilometres. DART proved the basic principle, but it also produced a puzzle: the deflection was considerably larger than computer simulations had predicted. One leading explanation is that the debris blasted off the surface acted like the exhaust of a rocket, adding extra push beyond the spacecraft's own momentum. Yet to estimate how much extra push a future impact might deliver, scientists need to know what Dimorphos is made of, how massive it is and how its surface responded, information that DART, destroyed in the collision, could not provide.

This is where Hera, launched on 7 October 2024, comes in. Over the coming months it will carry out what ESA calls a "crash-site investigation." It will measure Dimorphos's mass, map the crater or reshaping caused by the impact, and examine the asteroid's internal structure using visual, laser and radio instruments. It will also release two shoebox-sized satellites, known as CubeSats. One, Milani, will analyse the minerals on the surface, while the other, Juventas, will attempt the first radar sounding of an asteroid's interior. The first detailed images of Dimorphos are expected on 25 November 2026.

Supporters argue that such work is an inexpensive insurance policy. Large impacts are rare, but their consequences can be severe. In 1908 an object exploded over Tunguska in Siberia and flattened around 2,000 square kilometres of forest, and in 2013 a meteor that burst above Chelyabinsk, Russia, injured more than a thousand people, mostly through shattered glass. Because the probability of a dangerous impact in any given year is low while the potential damage is enormous, advocates contend that a planet able to deflect asteroids should test its methods before an emergency, not during one.

Skeptics raise several objections. Some question whether money spent on rare threats would save more lives if it were directed toward pressing problems such as disease or adaptation to climate change. Others note that results from one asteroid may not apply to another. Many small asteroids appear to be loose "rubble piles" held together by weak gravity, and a body with a different structure might fragment rather than move as a whole, possibly creating several hazardous objects instead of one. There are also questions of governance. If a deflection effort shifted an asteroid's predicted impact point from one country toward another along the way, who would have the authority to make that decision?

These concerns are serious, but they arguably strengthen rather than weaken the case for missions like Hera. Uncertainty about how different asteroids respond is exactly the knowledge gap the mission is designed to narrow, and the cost of planetary-defence research is modest compared with the damage a single regional impact could cause. Questions of governance, meanwhile, are best addressed calmly and in advance, using real data rather than speculation. A single pixel may seem a small reward for a two-year journey, but it marks the beginning of a far more detailed answer to an old question: whether humanity could ever change the course of a threatening object in space.

articles.title: Who Wrote This? Artificial Intelligence and the Purpose of Homework
articles.dek: Most British pupils who use AI don't admit it. Should schools ban it, or ask what homework is really for?
paras: A survey published in early November 2026 has added fresh evidence to one of the most heated debates in education. According to the Future of Education Report 2026, produced by the tutoring company GoStudent and covering six European countries, 73 percent of British pupils who use artificial intelligence (AI) at school had not acknowledged its role in their work. Among pupils who use AI for schoolwork, 58 percent said they submitted AI-generated material as their own at least once a week, the highest proportion of the six countries surveyed. Only 28 percent said they had ever received a structured lesson on how to use AI properly.

Teachers' responses were equally striking. Ninety-four percent said they knew that pupils were handing in AI-generated work, and two-thirds said it happened at least weekly. Perhaps more worrying, 44 percent were not confident that most of their pupils could write a complete essay from scratch without AI assistance. The concern has reached the top of the exam system. The chief regulator of Ofqual, England's exams watchdog, has written to exam boards about AI misuse in coursework, noting that although the number of detected cases remains relatively low, the true extent of the problem is a cause for concern.

The British figures echo trends elsewhere. In the United States, a RAND Corporation survey of young people aged 12 to 29 found that the share using AI for homework rose from 48 percent to 62 percent between May and December 2025, with middle and high school students driving most of the increase. Interestingly, students themselves expressed doubts: 67 percent agreed that relying heavily on AI for schoolwork harms critical thinking, an increase of more than ten percentage points in less than a year. Many also reported confusion, saying that the rules depended on which teacher they had, and some worried about being falsely accused of cheating.

Such numbers should be interpreted with care. Surveys depend on self-reporting, and definitions of "using AI" vary widely, from asking a chatbot to explain a difficult concept to copying an entire essay. Moreover, GoStudent sells tutoring services, including AI-based ones, so it has a commercial interest in presenting the situation as a problem that requires expert guidance. None of this means the findings are wrong, but it does suggest that the exact percentages matter less than the overall pattern: AI use is widespread, rules are unclear, and teachers are uneasy.

Responses to this pattern fall broadly into two camps. The first emphasises academic integrity. Its supporters argue that if pupils can outsource homework to a machine, homework no longer measures what pupils know, and grades lose their meaning. They favour clear bans for certain tasks, more supervised writing in class, and a return to handwritten or oral assessments. The second camp contends that prohibition is both unrealistic and short-sighted. AI tools will be part of almost every workplace these pupils enter, so schools should teach them to use those tools critically: to check facts, question outputs and disclose assistance honestly. As GoStudent's chief executive put it, "The key is teaching them to use it critically."

Each side has a point, and each has a weakness. Strict bans are difficult to enforce, since AI-generated text is hard to detect reliably, and heavy reliance on detection software risks punishing honest students, which is precisely the fear expressed by the American pupils. On the other hand, "teaching critical use" assumes that pupils already possess the basic skills needed to judge an AI's output. A student who has never learned to build an argument independently may not recognise when a machine's argument is weak.

Perhaps the more productive question is not whether AI should be allowed but what homework is for. If the purpose of an assignment is practice, strengthening a skill through effort, then letting a machine do it defeats the purpose, much as sending a robot to the gym would do nothing for one's own fitness. If, however, the purpose is to produce a polished product, then AI may be a legitimate tool, provided its use is acknowledged. Schools that clearly distinguish between these two types of task, and explain the reasons to pupils, may achieve more than either blanket bans or unlimited freedom. The survey results suggest that, at present, most pupils have been told neither.

Some teachers want to ban AI from homework completely, while others want students to use AI openly as long as they explain how they used it. Which policy is better for students' learning, and why?
